data.title: Expanding on naval blockade, U.S. military looks to restrict Iranian land commerce
data.description:
Expanding on naval blockade, US military looks to restrict Iranian land commerce

By Phil Stewart
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 4:51 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

(Adds dropped word in paragraph 12)

By Phil Stewart

WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Building on a months-long naval blockade on Iran, the US military said on Saturday it is launching a task force to help crack ‌down on Tehran's movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material over its land borders and through the ‌Caspian Sea.

Task Force Iron Gate, which was first reported by Reuters, will be based in Tampa, Florida, and will coordinate with other US government agencies. ​Beyond movement of weapons, it will also focus on halting the flow of dual-use technologies used by Iran and stemming what Washington calls illegal revenue streams.

Advertisement

The establishment of the task force is the latest illustration of how the US is still searching for ways to increase pressure on Tehran, more than eight months after launching with Israel a war against the Islamic Republic.

While US ‌strikes have dealt devastating blows to Iran's conventional ⁠military and the US naval blockade has severely restricted its crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea, Iran still poses a formidable threat to the region and its ⁠rulers have tightened their grip on the country.

IRAN'S SECRET NETWORK

A Reuters investigation found Iran has created a secret network of military agencies to import at least $2 billion in hardware, explosives and heavy-duty trucks since January 2025, evading both the US naval blockade and Western ​sanctions.

The ​material entered Iran by cargo ship across the Caspian Sea from ​Russia, by truck from Central Asia, and by freight ‌planes from China, the Reuters investigation showed.

US Central Command said the task force will coordinate with other government agencies. A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that was expected to include the Treasury, State and Justice Departments but also the intelligence community.

"Strengthening CENTCOM's collaboration with US interagency partners will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military," Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of Central Command, said in a statement.

Central Command estimated that its ‌naval blockade has prevented Iran from exporting more than $25 billion in ​crude oil.

Still, Iran has proven resilient and gloated following US midterm election ​results that punished Trump's Republican Party, giving control of ​Congress to opposition Democrats. Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for electoral rout, and ‌appeared to question whether the conflict was worth it.

Mediators ​have intensified efforts in recent ​days to end the war between Iran and the United States amid fears it could reignite after the US midterm elections.

Trump has been threatening to carry out a new offensive against Iran, putting countries in the Gulf ​on edge, since Tehran has threatened broad ‌retaliation against Gulf infrastructure.

Reuters has reported that US intelligence assessments in recent months have indicated that renewed strikes ​on Iran would not fundamentally change Tehran's negotiating position or lead to the fall of Iran's government.

(Reporting ​by Phil Stewart; Editing by Andrew Heavens and Tomasz Janowski)

data.title: Trump ally Laura Loomer reportedly charged up to $5,000 for political posts
data.description:
Trump ally Loomer was paid thousands for political tweets, people familiar say

Drew Harwell and Scott Nover, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
Updated Sat, November 7, 2026 at 4:47 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The right-wing activist Laura Loomer has been paid by private clients to make political posts on social media without publicly disclosing the payments, according to a former campaign aide to President Donald Trump and three others familiar with the arrangements, shedding light on what they say is a business practice of one of the Trump administration's most influential online firebrands.

The allegations were made by Alex Bruesewitz, an adviser to Trump's 2024 campaign, and three other people who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Two of the three people said they had paid Loomer directly to post political messages on her X account, where she has 1.9 million followers. The third said they had overseen clients who paid her to post on the account. The three spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.

Advertisement

Bank transaction emails and a wire transfer statement reviewed by The Washington Post appear to show four payments totaling more than $60,000 sent to Loomer and a Florida-based company registered in her name, King Breaker Media, since May of last year.

The documents do not specify the purpose of the payments, but two people familiar with the arrangements said they were for political posts.

Loomer, one of Trump's best-known online acolytes, denied to The Post that she is paid to post on social media. She instead described herself as a journalist and activist and disputed the idea that she is an influencer paid to promote any political cause.

The new claims about Loomer's influence business could add fuel to a growing debate about the little-regulated industry of political messaging on social media, where influencers on both sides of the aisle have operated in a legal gray area between advocacy and advertising.

Bruesewitz first posted his allegations on X on Thursday. Many of the details about Loomer's alleged online influence operation have not been previously reported.

Bruesewitz said in an interview with The Post that he had paid Loomer for tweets last year. He said the money had been sent through his political consulting firm, X Strategies, for posts related to policy issues. He declined to specify what clients.

Despite brokering these deals himself, he believes that they should require clearer disclosures and have "gotten out of hand."

Loomer disputed Bruesewitz's account and said that his firm contacted her last year offering to pay her for research.

"He paid me to make a one-page research document for him, and then he wanted me to distribute the information. And that's what I did," Loomer said. Asked where she was expected to distribute the research, she said, "Either X or maybe an article."

When asked how that was different from being paid to tweet, Loomer said she had actually been told to create the research document but that Bruesewitz had said he would have it distributed.

Loomer accused Bruesewitz of "lashing out" at her because of her political beliefs.

Bruesewitz and the three other people declined to publicly share the tweets they said Loomer had published to maintain the privacy of their clients. But The Post reviewed a selection of the tweets under the condition that they not be revealed publicly.

Two of the people said that Loomer charges $3,000 to $5,000 per tweet, and sometimes more.

Loomer said she does not have set pricing for consulting work. "I certainly don't charge $5,000 for a tweet," she said.

The four people who had paid or oversaw payments to Loomer for posting political statements on social media said she is an effective, if sometimes unpredictable, messenger and a key way of trying to get a line directly to Trump.

Jared Holt, a senior researcher at Open Measures, a platform that measures the spread of online extremism and disinformation, agreed. "This is somebody that has a tremendous amount of influence and access to the president's ear," said Holt, who studies the far right.

Loomer said in an interview Thursday night that she could not discuss the terms of her work with most of her clients due to confidentiality agreements and the fact that her accountant handled her invoices.

"I'm not some influencer that makes money from tweeting. My business is public affairs and opposition research," she said. "I also have a media company. It's not illegal to make a living in America."

Roughly one hour after The Post discussed the claims with Loomer, she announced on X that she is taking a hiatus from her online show, "Loomer Unleashed," so she could pursue a more "healthy work life balance" and prepare for her upcoming wedding.

"I just need to step back, recharge, refocus, and be present in my own life and my own mind with peace and clarity for a little while," she wrote. Loomer said the announcement had been scheduled in advance.

Loomer, 33, has traveled with Trump and met privately with him in the Oval Office during his second term in office. Detractors within the administration have taken issue with Loomer's relationship to the president and have lamented that several high-ranking defense and national security officials have been dismissed after she has publicly rebuked them, often on her X account.

Trump last year called Loomer a "very nice person" and a "patriot." After the White House fired aides on the National Security Council staff last year whom Loomer had accused of disloyalty, Trump denied that she was involved in the dismissal but acknowledged she had made some firing recommendations and said, "Sometimes I listen to those recommendations."

The White House declined to comment.

The Federal Trade Commission requires bloggers, influencers and other online figures to disclose when they have been paid to endorse a product, but the agency doesn't have jurisdiction over political ads.

Some advocacy groups have called for stronger regulations around paid political content. The Campaign Legal Center last year petitioned the Federal Election Commission to consider requiring "paid for by" disclosures on influencers' political posts, saying they could help voters better assess the content they see online. California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed legislation that will penalize influencers who post paid political messages without disclosure.

The general lack of transparency among political influencers, Holt said, "further degrades confidence in what people see online and how genuine it may be, or how representative it may actually be of the communities that these various influencers purport to speak for."

Loomer has frequently said her bulldog advocacy reflects her genuine views, telling The Bulwark in May 2025 that she was "not paid for [her] posts."

One person who said they had paid Loomer to tweet on behalf of clients said she was deliberate in her work and would only tweet if she agreed with the position. The person said not every client wanted to work with her because they believed she was polarizing but that some had hired her assuming she had an audience in the White House.

The person added, however, that Loomer was like a "nuclear bomb." "You have to be careful how to use that," they said. "It's effective but also turns a lot of things to s--- if you're not careful."

Loomer said she took that as a compliment. "I'm glad people find me to be effective and think I have a good reach," she said. "I'm not going to apologize for monetizing the fact that people fear me."

data.title: House Democrats will start their majority focused on healthcare and ending the Iran war
data.description:
House Democrats will start their majority focused on boosting healthcare and ending the Iran war

KEVIN FREKING
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 1:09 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Election 2026

1 of 6
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a election night event at a hotel on Capitol Hill in Washington, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite)

WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democratic leaders are placing an early emphasis on healthcare as they discuss their immediate priorities upon the swearing-in of the new Congress on Jan. 3.

Early votes in the House next year are expected to focus on boosting Medicaid and restoring an enhanced tax subsidy that is designed to lower the cost of Affordable Care Act health plans for millions of enrollees.

Democrats are also promising swift action on legislation to stop the war with Iran and to reverse some of President Donald Trump'strade tariffs.

Advertisement

"We're going to get out of the gate fast," said New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader who is in line to become the next House speaker.

The legislative flurry carries enormous stakes for Democrats as they seek to translate their sweeping victories in the midterms — their numbers will exceed 250 in the 435-member House — into achievements that deliver on their promises to lower the cost of living.

Obstacles abound for the Democratic agenda

Passing those bills should not be a problem with such a large Democratic House majority. Getting them signed into law most certainly could be.

A 60-vote threshold in the Senate looms for the legislation, as does a potential presidential veto. Trump on election night posted a photo on his social media site of a red hat with a simple message on it: "VETO".

Following those early votes, Jeffries said five working groups are developing plans to put forward bills that would lower costs in areas such as housing, energy, groceries and caregiving.

Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., said Democrats will at some point take up legislation dealing with artificial intelligence and data centers. He is part of a group of lawmakers working on a document that will lay out some of the priorities for Jeffries to consider.

"House Republicans last year made a conscious decision to let the AI industry run wild, and that was a bad decision politically and a bad decision on policy," Lieu said. "Two things will change next term. We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails on AI, and specifically data centers."

New Congress will return to past political fights

Democrats are trying to reverse Medicaid changes that are expected to cut more than $900 billion from the program over a decade. The Republican-approved cuts helped offset some of the costs of Trump's big tax and spending cut bill that was signed into law last year. The Medicaid changes in the bill imposed new administrative requirements and added conditions for eligibility, including work requirements.

Some of the most substantial changes have yet to take effect. Still, enrollment in Medicaid has dropped by about 5 million, or about 7% since July 2025, when the bill was signed into law, according to KFF, a health policy research and news organization.

Reversing those cuts would likely require Trump and the Republicans to abandon the hard-fought changes they made to cut entitlement spending in their signature tax bill. It's an unlikely proposition.

The effort to extend enhanced tax subsidies for certain enrollees in ACA plans has also been debated and voted on in the current Congress. The measure passed the House with some Republican support but stalled in the Senate.

There also have been numerous war powers votes regarding Iran — 14 in the Senate and six in the House.

Gridlock may be on the horizon

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said going into the election that a Democratic majority in the next Congress would amount to "two years of paralysis."

"I don't think that's good for anybody," Thune said.

But Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York is insisting that Democrats will push their agenda with or without the Republican president's help.

"If he vetoes it, it will show the divisions. As much as we didn't want to shut down, when we shut down the government for a month over healthcare, people knew we were on their side," Schumer said in an interview with The New York Times' podcast "The Daily."

Schumer said he believes Democrats can gain some Republican votes on restoring the enhanced subsidies for ACA plans. When asked if he was hearing from Republicans expressing a willingness to work with him on legislation, he replied: "They're never so definitive but, yes, I am getting initial signs that way on certain issues, not on every issue."

While the prospects for getting any of the early priority bills over the finish line are uncertain, the votes in Congress will help frame the choices voters will face during a presidential election in 2028.

Tensions exist within the new Democratic majority

Progressive groups call the agenda outlined by Jeffries a good early start, but they have much greater expectations for Democrats this Congress.

"It's perfectly fine if the Senate and the House are unified and Donald Trump is standing in the way because that sets up another tidal wave election in 2028," said Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, a Democratic-aligned group that backs progressive candidates and policies.

At the same time, he said Schumer cannot be content to let bills die in the Senate because of the 60-vote threshold.

"It will require the Democrats to get rid of the filibuster," Green said. "There's no doubt about it."

He said there's a disparity because Republicans' top priorities — tax cuts and Supreme Court justices — can get through with simple majorities. But the Democratic Party's top priorities require 60 votes to overcome a filibuster.

"The only question is will the American public trust Democrats enough to keep giving us more power or will this week's gains whittle away because we do nothing? That's why the filibuster is a threshold question," Green said.

Schumer in an interview with The Associated Press this week would not say whether he would try and eliminate the filibuster.

"The focus has got to be on getting things done," Schumer said. "That's all I am saying."

In a memo to fellow members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, said Democrats also need to target what he called "powerful forces outside of government." Examples he cited were corporations using Americans' private data to adjust their pricing based on a consumer's personal data and AI companies that he says are putting jobs and lives at risk.

"By focusing not just on the Trump administration but also on big corporations and billionaires, we will show the American people we are not just anti-Trump but also pro-worker and pro-consumer," Casar said.

___

Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

data.title: Stephen Miller pushed for 3,000 ICE arrests a day. Now he's Trump's chief of staff.
data.description:
Politics

Stephen Miller, Trump's new chief of staff, is the architect of his controversial immigration policies

By
Nicole Sganga
Homeland Security and Justice Correspondent
Nicole Sganga is CBS News' homeland security and justice correspondent. She is based in Washington, D.C., and reports for all shows and platforms.
Read Full Bio
Nicole Sganga,
Caitlin Yilek
Politics Reporter
Caitlin Yilek is a politics reporter at CBSNews.com, based in Washington, D.C. She previously worked for the Washington Examiner and The Hill, and was a member of the 2022 Paul Miller Washington Reporting Fellowship with the National Press Foundation.
Read Full Bio
Caitlin Yilek

November 6, 2026 / 8:36 PM EST / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Washington — Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations. 

Mr. Trump announced the staffing shake-up on Friday, calling Miller one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who has been his chief of staff throughout his second term. 

The move comes after Republicans suffered crippling losses in the midterm elections and as Democrats plan sweeping investigations into the administration's actions, including its immigration enforcement policies. 

Miller was the architect behind many of those policies and also championed the administration's immigration enforcement expansion, which has been supported by approximately $170 billion that congressional Republicans allocated for immigration enforcement and border security in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025. 

During Mr. Trump's first term, Miller helped develop and publicly defend the administration's executive order that restricted entry by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban led to protests around the U.S. and legal challenges. A third iteration of the ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018. 

He was a leading supporter of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance immigration policy, which resulted in thousands of family separations, and he pressed for dramatic reductions in refugee admissions. The administration repeatedly lowered the annual refugee admissions ceiling, ultimately setting it at 15,000 for fiscal year 2021, a record low at the time.

Miller also advocated penalizing legal immigrants who received public benefits and making it harder for them to obtain citizenship.  

In Mr. Trump's second term, Miller pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to make at least 3,000 immigration arrests per day. In May 2025, Miller publicly demanded a dramatic increase in daily arrests, placing pressure on ICE leadership and expanding enforcement beyond immigrants who had been convicted of serious crimes. 

He also proposed that the National Guard be deployed to support mass deportations. 

Miller's arrest targets were part of a sweeping expansion of enforcement in communities, workplaces and immigration courts. Detentions of immigrants without criminal histories rose sharply, and increased ICE activity sparked protests across the country.  

The longtime Trump adviser also championed the use of a wartime law — the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — to bypass due process and quickly deport alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador, where they were held in a notorious maximum-security prison, known as CECOT. The deportations set off a legal battle, and the Supreme Court blocked the government from immediately deporting the Venezuelans without giving them an opportunity to challenge their removal. 

As part of the administration's deportation efforts, Miller has supported an aggressive expansion of third-country deportations. The administration has deported immigrants to countries where they have no citizenship or family ties, including several African nations. 

In May 2025, Miller said the administration was actively considering suspending the constitutional mechanism that allows detainees to challenge their confinement in court. 

At a March 2026 conference in Miami, Miller argued that military force, rather than traditional criminal law enforcement alone, was needed to defeat cartels. 

Miller appeared alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office this summer as he signed executive orders to refuse citizenship to some children born in the United States, after the Supreme Court struck down his earlier executive order aiming to end birthright citizenship.

data.title: Trump picks Stephen Miller as chief of staff, signaling intent to stay the course
data.description:
Trump makes hardliner Stephen Miller his chief of staff after midterm defeat

By Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland and Trevor Hunnicutt
Updated Fri, November 6, 2026 at 10:57 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland and Trevor Hunnicutt

WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his chief of staff on Friday, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress.

Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront ‌a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration.

Advertisement

A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a moment when the Republican Party's defeat in Tuesday's ‌midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda.

In a social media post, Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors," and praised Wiles for doing "an outstanding job." Trump said the change would take effect on Monday.

A White House official said Miller's appointment signals ​that Trump has no intention of rethinking his policies and instead is rewarding his most loyal aides.

"He's not changing course," the official said, despite tens of millions of American voters repudiating Trump's domestic agenda and foreign policy.

Trump said this week he was willing to work with Democrats on Capitol Hill. But elevating Miller, who is known for being caustic and uncompromising, could signal a more confrontational approach and a renewed push to advance the president's agenda on immigration and other issues, several White House officials said.

Trump had been displeased with his political and communications operations in the run-up to Tuesday's election as his public approval ratings fell near record lows. This week, he said the White House needed to be "more aggressive" as Democrats retake congressional power, ‌according to a person briefed on the matter.

"The mission now is more clear than ⁠ever," Miller said on X after his appointment. "Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic."

Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become the new Democratic speaker of the House, responded to the announcement by calling Miller a "reckless extremist" in a posting on X.

MILLER DRIVING IMMIGRATION CRACKDOWN

Miller, 41, is one of Trump's longest-serving aides and one of ⁠only a few who served throughout his first and second terms in office.

Since Trump's return to the White House in 2025, Miller has officially served as deputy chief of staff under Wiles, but he has wielded outsize influence across much of Trump's domestic agenda and has had the president's ear.

He is perhaps best known for driving Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown, setting a goal of 3,000 arrests a day. The efforts to meet that target pushed masked US immigration officers into communities around the country, increasingly arresting people with no criminal ​records ​and who had been living in the country for decades.

The crackdown, however, gets poor marks with Americans. Just 36% of respondents to ​a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed early this week approve of it, with 54% disapproving.

Representative Robert Garcia, ‌the top Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, said the party planned to investigate Miller's immigration policies. "Stephen Miller should lawyer up," he said.

Miller was also deeply involved in Trump's campaign to remake the federal bureaucracy, which led to the dismissal of tens of thousands of civil servants in 2025. He was also a driving force behind the administration's battles with universities, diversity programs and other institutions.

HAWKISH FOREIGN POLICY

On foreign policy, Miller has been a vocal supporter of Trump's deadly military strikes on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean and Pacific, a campaign that has raised legal questions.

He has also praised US and Israeli strikes in Iran and defended a naval blockade and sanctions as ways to weaken Tehran and curb its ability to threaten its neighbors. It is not clear whether that is still his view after voters punished Republicans this week in part for the economic fallout from the Iran war.

Marc Short, who was chief ‌of staff to then-Vice President Mike Pence in Trump's first term, said that in Miller, Trump is "getting someone who is wed to him" ​and who is willing to battle Congress over issues like immigration and congressional investigations.

"It would not suggest that there is high expectation for bipartisan ​legislation," Short said in an interview.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who faces Democratic calls for impeachment over the ​Iran war, celebrated Miller's promotion with a social media post reading, "Patriots in control," reflecting the enthusiasm of some Trump allies for putting Miller in a position of greater authority.

SHAKE UP AFTER ELECTION ‌SETBACK

The chief of staff typically wields great influence as the president's gatekeeper. The person ​manages White House staff, organizes the president's time and schedule, and ​oversees other government departments and lawmakers.

Wiles, 69, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night, will move to Trump's political operation, according to a White House official.

The veteran political operative from Florida was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff.

She brought decades of political experience to the role and was regarded as running a more disciplined operation than some of Trump's prior top aides. She maintained her role even ​while undergoing treatment earlier this year for early-stage breast cancer.

Wiles rarely challenged Trump's policies ‌but brought discipline to an often chaotic operation and was seen as a voice of reason. Her exit raises questions about who will play her role.

Trump ran through four chiefs of staff – an unusually ​high number – during his 2017-2021 term, as they were seen to have struggled to rein in the unpredictable president.

data.title: Democrats take full control of Arizona government for 1st time in 60 years
data.description:
Democrats win the Arizona House, Senate and governor’s office for the first time since 1966

Associated Press
Updated Fri, November 6, 2026 at 6:39 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Election 2026 Arizona House

1 of 3
Arizona Democratic House candidate JoAnna Mendoza reacts at an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Tucson, Ariz. (AP Photo/Ross D. Franklin) (AP Photo/Ross D. Franklin)

PHOENIX (AP) — Democrats in Arizona won control of both legislative chambers and retained the governor's office, giving the party its first trifecta in the state since 1966 as Democrats made major gains nationwide in this week's elections and took control of both chambers of Congress.

In her first term, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed more than 540 measures passed by the Republican-led Legislature on policies including taxes, immigration and voting laws. Hobbs has said she's looking to address water issues and affordability, and take on fraud and abuse in the state's school voucher program.

The Associated Press called enough legislative races to confirm that both chambers flipped on Friday. The news organization calls races individually and it can take several days after voting, depending on when election officials tally the votes and how close the elections are. There have not been major disputes or disruptions this year.

Advertisement

In Arizona, Republicans have held the House for 60 years and the Senate since the early 1990s.

Overall, Democrats took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors' offices — in at least six states where they previously shared power with Republicans. Besides Arizona, those wins were in the battleground states of Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Wisconsin.

The flips weren't just in states that are normally competitive. Democrats won control of the Texas House, which Republicans have held since 2003, and elected Gina Hinojosa as the state's first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994. Republicans held onto the state Senate.

Democrats also flipped the lower chambers of the legislatures in Maine and North Carolina and both chambers in New Hampshire, where Republican Kelly Ayotte was reelected. The count could grow as results are tallied in additional states.

The National Council of State Legislatures says it's likely to end up as the election with the most legislative seats and chambers changing parties since the 2010 election, when Republicans took over governments across the country amid the Great Recession.

Democrats will also hold the governor's office in at least 28 states. Results are still pending in Alaska and Kansas.

data.title: Cornell faculty votes 'no confidence' in university leaders over handling of rape allegations
data.description:
Cornell faculty vote ‘no confidence’ in university leadership after alleged fraternity gang rape

LEAH WILLINGHAM
Updated Fri, November 6, 2026 at 8:43 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Cornell Investigation

1 of 2
Students walk through Cornell University's campus, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, in Ithaca, N.Y. (AP Photo/Matt Burkhartt) (AP Photo/Matt Burkhartt)

Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring "no confidence" in the school's top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student's lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024.

The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon.

The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman's allegations properly and have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.

Advertisement

While the faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified.

The board of trustees said Friday that the vote reflected deep anger on campus and sent a "clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable," but added that Kotlikoff and his administration were the right leaders to "thoughtfully and comprehensively" address the issue.

"The Board fully supports President Kotlikoff and his administration as they continue to listen and act decisively in support of students," board chair Anne Smalling said in a statement. She cited expanded sexual assault prevention education, additional victim advocates and more staff at the university's Office of Civil Rights as evidence of the administration's response.

Thomas Giuffra, Jane Doe's attorney, said in a statement Friday that "we are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus."

Lawsuit sparked outrage on campus

The Cornell community has been distressed since mid-September, when a former student filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.

All of the men have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren't involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York's attorney general.

Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a monthslong Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write "reflection" papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times.

Kotlikoff also convened a task force to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations.

Some faculty members have criticized Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.

Paul Ortiz, a labor history professor who co-sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said last week that hundreds of students, staff, alumni and faculty approached the resolution's sponsors to emphasize that "the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg" and that "a veritable fortress of silence has been breached" around sexual violence since the resolution's introduction.

Cornell's president defended his leadership

Speaking to Faculty Senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution, Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing sexual assault and asked for more time to make changes.

Kotlikoff defended his leadership, arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell's reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions he had been indifferent to the woman's case, though he acknowledged only recently learning she had left Cornell.

Kotlikoff said the university needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely and left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life. He argued that decisions should be based on research and evidence rather than emotion.

Some professors had said faculty should wait to vote until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine both how Cornell responded to the woman's initial rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports from other students.

The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff's resignation.

2 Justice Department officials resign, including US attorney who oversaw 'grand conspiracy' probe

ALANNA DURKIN RICHER and ERIC TUCKER
Updated Fri, November 6, 2026 at 6:45 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Miami who had been tasked with overseeing an investigation into foes of President Donald Trump has resigned, joining other high-profile Justice Department officials departing in the wake of the midterm elections, officials said Friday.

Jason Reding Quiñones' resignation follows frustrations among Washington officials with his management of the office assigned to lead the so-called "grand conspiracy" investigation, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues.

The Justice Department's top national security official, John Eisenberg, also resigned on Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said. On Thursday, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led a radical overhaul of the department's Civil Rights Division, also announced her departure.

Advertisement

Quiñones was confirmed by the Senate last year as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where the Justice Department had centered its meandering probe into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president.

His departure comes as the investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of several witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Blanche said in a social media post that the department is grateful for Quiñones' "leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro."

Castro, the former Cuban president, was indicted by Quiñones' office in May on charges related to the 1996 downing of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles.

Quiñones said Friday that he is leaving with "immense pride in what we accomplished together and profound gratitude for the opportunity to serve our great Nation."

"I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law," Quiñones wrote in a social media post.

The "grand conspiracy" investigation has proceeded in fits and starts for over a year with repeated setbacks and departures. Last April, a lead national security prosecutor in the investigation of former CIA Director John Brennan was replaced on the team after raising questions about the strength of the case.

Shortly afterward, Joseph diGenova, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, took over the probe. DiGenova resigned from the Justice Department in September without bringing any criminal charges.

Eisenberg was sworn in as assistant attorney general in charge of the department's National Security Division in June 2025 and oversaw cases involving espionage, terrorism, export control violations, cyber crimes and other matters.

Among the division's most high-profile cases under his watch was the prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton, who pleaded guilty this year to allegations of mishandling classified information and is awaiting sentencing.

"He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation's ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic," Blanche said in a statement.

data.title: Meghan Markle's father Thomas arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse material
data.description:
Meghan Markle's father, Thomas, arrested by FBI on charges linked to child sexual abuse material

The U.S. Attorney's Office for California said Thomas Markle was charged with one count of "possession of child pornography."

Harriet Sinclair
Updated Fri, November 6, 2026 at 5:14 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Meghan Markle's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was arrested in Florida on Friday on charges related to child sexual abuse material, authorities said.

Markle, 82, was arrested by the FBI at a care home near Tampa, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California said in a press release. He was charged with one count of possession of child pornography.

Authorities said Markle was arrested after agents discovered approximately 78 items — including slides, film negatives, and books — that contained suspected child sexual abuse material (CSAM) while searching two storage units registered to Markle, at least one of which was in the Los Angeles area.

Advertisement

"Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said. "These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law."

The statement said that, in October 2026, law enforcement learned that an individual signed an affidavit regarding the discovery of suspected CSAM among Markle's possessions in the Philippines. Officers then interviewed a separate individual who revealed Markle had rented a storage unit in the Los Angeles area.

This led to the discovery of a second storage unit. Both had been rented by Markle since 2008.

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that "Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions."

"This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide," Patel added.

If convicted, Markle would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison. He is expected to appear in court in Tampa on Friday.

"This case highlights the importance of the involvement of the public, even if it's a family member or close friend, to be vigilant and speak up if they have information on individuals they suspect may be preying on and exploiting our children," said Patrick Grandy, the assistant director in charge of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office.

In October, it was reported that Markle was under investigation in the Philippines over allegations that he possessed child sexual abuse material. He has not been charged by police in the Philippines.

The Sun first reported that his son, Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jr., told Philippine police that after his father left the country in May, he discovered images of child sexual abuse material among boxes at his father's former home in Cebu.

Markle Sr. denied those allegations, telling the Daily Mail on Oct. 23: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick."

Markle is believed to have returned to the U.S. in May, after his left leg was amputated in the Philippines in December 2025. In October, The Sun reported Markle moved into Maravida Senior Living care home, a facility which specializes in "memory care."

Meghan Markle released a statement following the claims, saying she was "deeply distressed." She also revealed that in 2019 she received a copy of a letter containing "troubling" allegations about him, which had been sent to London's Metropolitan Police.

"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said. British police subsequently said it had not shared the letter with other law enforcement agencies.

According to the Sun on Sunday, Meghan was advised that speaking publicly could jeopardize any potential legal case.

Addressing her decision to keep Archie and Lilibet away from their grandfather over the past few years, Meghan said that "any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them."

She added: "My sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."

Meghan reportedly wrote to her estranged father in December 2025 to tell him she was aware of child abuse allegations against him and would not allow him to meet his grandchildren. Meghan reportedly told her father the letter would be the last time he heard from her.
